domain_label: Game-Feel & Real-Time Motion — Juice, Principles & Motion Curves
purpose: A method for authoring the FEEL of the opt-in water-drop fluency drill — the drop's fall/gravity/easing, the water rise/surface, the decay animation curve, splash/particle/squash-stretch polish, and the ack/reward-beat choreography — grounded in game-feel doctrine, the classic animation principles, and the bezier/spring curve vocabulary, with every external claim labelled and every feel constant deferred to measured tuning.
assumptions: no observed dataset, playtest telemetry, or device motion benchmark is supplied; all scores are heuristic priors
external game-feel and animation sources are snippet-grade (direct WebFetch to the canonical publishers 403-blocked in this build env) and are tagged accordingly
the app ships no animation/physics library today, so every feel constant is UNKNOWN until prototyped on the target device
exclusions: the drill mechanic, reward logic, rise-per-hit/decay-rate constants, and reward psychology (owned by engage)
the static visual encoding — step count, hue token, colorblind redundancy, tank form (owned by viz)
the reduced-motion/accessibility contract and the honesty copy (developed in kb2 and owned with uxguide)
the render-performance envelope, frame budget, and library build-vs-adopt verdict (developed in kb3)
which items are drill-eligible and the ESL-readable floor value itself (owned by qcraft)

competency_questions.question: What is game feel, how does it decompose into real-time control, simulated space, and polish, and how does that frame scope graphux to the drill's feel only?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: states the Swink decomposition, attributes it as a snippet-grade source, and scopes graphux to feel with mechanic/encoding/copy as inputs

competency_questions.question: What is the real-time response target for control to feel responsive, and how is the tap acknowledgement separated from the reward beat?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names the ~100ms ack target (tagged for source-verify) and separates ack latency from reward-beat pacing

competency_questions.question: What is 'juice', what is the counter-current of restraint, and what is graphux's polish budget for the drill?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: defines juice with its GDC source, states the restraint counter-current, and lists the splash/ripple/squash-stretch/optional-haptic budget

competency_questions.question: Which classic animation principles govern the drop/water/splash, and what does volume-conserving squash-and-stretch require?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: names squash-stretch, anticipation, and easing from the 12 principles and states volume conservation, with the attribution tagged

competency_questions.question: How do bezier easing curves and spring physics differ, and how does graphux decide between them per motion?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: defines cubic-bezier and mass/stiffness/damping springs, notes the CSS linear() bridge, and frames the per-motion measured choice

competency_questions.question: How is the drop's fall shaped, and why can graphux own its SHAPE but not its DURATION?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: specifies an ease-in gravity shape and states the duration is floored by qcraft's ESL window, never shortened for feel

competency_questions.question: How does the water rise and decay animate while staying on viz's quantized honest steps and honest momentum framing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: animates between discrete steps with an ease-out settle and frames decay as session momentum, not forgetting

competency_questions.question: Why must every drill motion map to a real event, and what does that forbid?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: requires each motion to bind to a genuine event and forbids feedback on speed/motion alone or mastery-implying flourishes

competency_questions.question: Why are the drill's feel constants UNKNOWN until tuned, and how are external motion claims labelled?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: marks feel constants UNKNOWN-until-tuned on the target device and labels external claims FACT-source/UNVERIFIED-SOURCE

competency_questions.question: How does graphux keep polish from becoming a reward economy or obscuring the information the drill conveys?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: applies the restraint rule and legibility dominance so juice serves confirmation and never buries the choice or level read

glossary.definition: The real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space with interactions emphasised by polish, decomposed into real-time control, simulated space, and polish/juice [FACT-source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_feel — snippet-grade, direct fetch 403-blocked].

The polish layer of particles, screenshake, sound, and animation layered onto an interaction to make it feel alive; not free, and must serve the interaction rather than obscure it [FACT-source: GDC Europe 2012 'Juice it or lose it' — snippet-grade].
The animation principle that conveys weight, mass, and flexibility while conserving volume — an object flattening on impact must widen [FACT-source: 12 basic principles of animation — snippet-grade].
The principle of placing more frames at the ends of a move so motion accelerates and decelerates rather than moving linearly; the drop eases in, the rise eases out.

A timing curve defined by four control points approximating a curve, the standard portable way to name an easing shape without hardcoding constants [FACT-source: joshwcomeau spring-physics — snippet-grade].

A motion model parameterised by mass, stiffness, and damping that produces a decaying oscillation with no fixed end-time; gives the most lifelike settle but an open-ended, pacing-risky duration [FACT-source: joshwcomeau — snippet-grade].

A multi-point CSS timing function that samples a spring curve into many points to approximate spring feel where a true spring is not used [FACT-source: carmenansio spring-physics-css — snippet-grade].
The deliberately longer feedback sequence (water rise + splash) that confirms outcome, sequenced after a fast sub-~100ms control acknowledgement.
The honest framing of the meter's decay as 'use it or lose it this session' — never forgetting or retrievability, never spanning days [FACT — GAMIFICATION_PLAN §1].

The set of tunable feel parameters (fall ease, rise stiffness, decay curve, splash scale, ack latency) whose values are UNKNOWN until measured on the target device and bounded by the honesty/ESL/perf contracts.

nodes.definition: Frame the aesthetic layer: game feel is the real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space with interactions emphasised by polish, decomposed into real-time control, simulated space, and polish (the 'juice') [FACT-source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_feel]. graphux owns ONLY the FEEL of the opt-in water-drop fluency drill under this frame; the mechanic (engage), the static encoding (viz), and the honesty copy (uxguide) are inputs it animates, never authors. This node fixes the vocabulary every other kb1 node refines.

included: game feel as control+simulation+polish over the drop/water/tank
the drill-only scope of the feel authority
excluded: the drill mechanic and reward logic (engage)

pros.claim: Naming feel as a decomposable construct makes each motion choice defensible against a feel criterion instead of taste
pros.example: asking whether a splash serves control-feedback, simulation, or polish before adding it

cons.claim: The frame front-loads game-feel theory before any drop is drawn, which can feel heavy for one small drill
cons.example: running the full decomposition for a single fade a convention would settle instantly

failure_modes: treating feel as decoration rather than real-time control of a simulated object
authoring the mechanic while claiming to only animate it
acceptance_tests: the frame states game feel as real-time control + simulated space + polish and scopes graphux to the drill feel only
revisit_triggers: a chosen animation library or a new drill surface revises the feel contract

base.update_signal: a chosen animation/physics library or a new drill type revises the feel contract

nodes.definition: For control to feel 'real-time' the correction/response cycle should acknowledge input under roughly 100 ms [FACT-source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_feel]. Applied to the drill: the tap on a STATIC option button must get an immediate visual acknowledgement this fast even when the reward beat (water rise, splash) is deliberately longer. Responsiveness of the ACK is separable from the pacing of the REWARD.

included: the sub-~100ms acknowledgement target for a tap
separating ACK latency from reward-beat duration
excluded: the fall-window duration itself (owned by the ESL floor, kb2)

pros.claim: A fast, separate ACK keeps the control loop feeling responsive without shortening the readable fall window
pros.example: flashing the chosen button instantly on tap while the water rise plays out over a longer beat

cons.claim: The ~100ms figure is a snippet-grade external claim, not a device-measured budget for this app
cons.example: quoting 100ms as a hard SLA when it should be verified against the target device

failure_modes: making the whole reward beat sub-100ms and thereby rushing the readable window
delaying the tap acknowledgement so the control feels laggy
acceptance_tests: ack of a static-button tap is specified to render under ~100ms, separate from the reward beat, with the number tagged for source-verify
revisit_triggers: a device measurement revises the perceived-responsiveness threshold

base.update_signal: device latency measurement revises the responsiveness target

nodes.definition: The drop, the water column, and the tank are virtual objects in a simulated space with position and velocity; feel comes from those quantities obeying a believable (not necessarily physically exact) motion model. This node is the aesthetic counterpart to viz's static tank — graphux moves the object viz shaped.

included: the drop/water/tank as position+velocity objects in a simulated space
believable over physically-exact motion
excluded: the static form and hue of the tank (viz)
the persisted meter value (there is none; kb2)

pros.claim: Modelling the drop as a moving object with velocity lets gravity, rise, and splash share one coherent simulation
pros.example: reusing the drop's fall velocity to scale the splash size so the two reads as one physical event

cons.claim: A simulation model invites physics the drill does not need and a library the app does not have
cons.example: adding fluid dynamics to a tank that only needs a stepped rise

failure_modes: over-simulating a decorative object into a performance and honesty liability
letting the simulated object become the click target
acceptance_tests: the drop/water/tank are specified as position+velocity objects with a believable motion model, not a physics engine
revisit_triggers: a physics library is prototyped and changes the feasible motion model

base.update_signal: a physics/animation library changes the feasible simulation model

nodes.definition: The 'juice' tradition (Jonasson & Purho, 'Juice it or lose it', GDC Europe 2012) iteratively layers particles, screenshake, sound, and animation onto a plain interaction to make it feel alive [FACT-source: https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/video-indies-resist-the-urge-to-juice-it-or-lose-it-]. graphux's polish budget for the drill is the splash, ripple, squash/stretch, and optional haptic/audio — each of which must map to a real event.

included: particles/shake/sound/animation as the polish layer
mapping each polish element to a real drill event
excluded: reward psychology and variable schedules (engage; REJECTED per plan)
copy and framing of the reward (uxguide)

pros.claim: A disciplined juice layer converts a flat correct/incorrect flip into a satisfying, legible confirmation
pros.example: a small splash + one ripple on a genuine correct-in-window hit rather than a bare number change

cons.claim: Juice is additive risk: it can obscure the information it is meant to confirm
cons.example: screenshake so strong it hides which option was chosen

failure_modes: adding juice that reads as reward for speed alone
stacking effects until the actual correctness signal is buried
acceptance_tests: the polish budget lists splash/ripple/squash-stretch/optional haptic-audio, each tied to a genuine event
revisit_triggers: a splash/particle element is found to obscure the correctness read and must be cut

base.update_signal: a usability check finds a polish element obscures the information it confirms

nodes.definition: The counter-current inside the juice community is 'resist the urge to juice it or lose it' — juice is not free and must SERVE the interaction, not decorate over it [FACT-source: https://roblog.co.uk/2024/03/juicy-games/]. For the drill this is doubly binding because juice that implies mastery or rewards speed violates the kb2 honesty contract. Restraint is the default; every effect earns its place.

included: juice must serve the interaction, not obscure it
restraint as the default posture for a study tool
excluded: the mastery-implication ban itself (kb2 owns it; this node points to it)

pros.claim: A restraint rule stops the drill from drifting into a slot-machine feel that the plan explicitly rejects
pros.example: cutting a celebratory burst that would read as durable progress rather than a session hit

cons.claim: Too much restraint can leave the drill feeling flat, undercutting the appeal that justified building it
cons.example: stripping so much polish that the fluency drill feels like a plain quiz and loses its draw

failure_modes: juicing until the tool feels like a reward economy
removing so much feel that the drill loses the appeal that motivated it
acceptance_tests: a restraint rule is stated: every effect must serve control-feedback or legible confirmation, tested against the honesty contract
revisit_triggers: an effect is added that serves no genuine event and must be justified or removed

base.update_signal: the honesty contract flags an effect as implying unearned mastery

nodes.definition: Thomas & Johnston's The Illusion of Life (1981) codifies 12 basic principles of animation [FACT-source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_basic_principles_of_animation]. The load-bearing subset for a falling drop, rising water, and a splash is squash-and-stretch, anticipation, and slow-in/slow-out (easing). These principles are the aesthetic grammar the drop's curves should obey.

included: the 12 principles and the drop-relevant subset
principles as the grammar for the drop/water/splash
excluded: the numeric easing constants (kb3 / feel tuning)
the full 12-principle catalogue beyond the drill subset

pros.claim: Grounding the drop in established principles gives objective handles (weight, anticipation, easing) for tuning feel
pros.example: using anticipation before the drop releases so its fall reads as intentional, not abrupt

cons.claim: The principles are hand-drawn-animation heuristics, not real-time-interaction laws, and can over-animate a UI micro-event
cons.example: adding full anticipation wind-up to a 200ms micro-interaction where it just adds latency

failure_modes: applying cinematic principles so heavily the interaction feels slow
ignoring the principles and producing lifeless linear motion
acceptance_tests: the drop-relevant subset (squash-stretch, anticipation, easing) is named and attributed to the 12 principles
revisit_triggers: a live source check revises the attribution or subset

base.update_signal: source verification revises the principle attribution

nodes.definition: Squash-and-stretch conveys weight, mass, and flexibility while CONSERVING VOLUME — an object squashing on impact must widen as it flattens [FACT-source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_basic_principles_of_animation]. It is the principle that makes the drop's fall and splash feel physical. Volume conservation is the honesty of the effect: a squash that also shrinks reads as wrong.

included: volume-conserving squash on the drop and splash
weight/mass/flexibility illusion
excluded: the water-level meaning of the splash (kb2)

pros.claim: Volume-conserving squash makes the drop's impact feel weighty and the splash believable
pros.example: widening the drop as it flattens on the water surface so mass is conserved on impact

cons.claim: Squash-stretch on a data-bearing meter risks distorting the value it encodes
cons.example: squashing the water column itself and momentarily misreading the stepped level

failure_modes: applying squash to the value-bearing water column and corrupting the read
non-volume-conserving squash that reads as an error
acceptance_tests: squash-stretch is specified as volume-conserving and applied to the drop/splash, never to the value-bearing level steps
revisit_triggers: a check finds squash applied to the encoded level and distorting the read

base.update_signal: a review finds squash distorting the encoded level

nodes.definition: Slow-in/slow-out (easing) places more frames at the ends of a move than the middle, so motion accelerates and decelerates rather than moving linearly [FACT-source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_basic_principles_of_animation]. The drop's fall should ease-in (accelerate under gravity); the water rise should ease-out (settle). Easing is where the curve vocabulary meets the animation principles.

included: easing as non-linear accel/decel for the fall and rise
the principle behind the drop's gravity curve

pros.claim: Easing turns a mechanical linear fall into a gravity-like, alive motion at zero information cost
pros.example: ease-in on the drop so it accelerates like a real falling droplet

cons.claim: An overly aggressive ease can make timing hard to read for the learner judging the window
cons.example: a heavy ease-in that makes the drop appear to hang then plunge unpredictably

failure_modes: linear motion that reads as robotic
an ease so extreme the fall timing becomes unpredictable
acceptance_tests: the fall is specified ease-in and the rise ease-out, grounded in the slow-in/slow-out principle
revisit_triggers: playtest finds the ease makes the fall-window timing hard to judge

base.update_signal: a playtest finds the ease harms window-timing legibility

nodes.definition: A cubic-bezier easing curve is defined by four control points approximating a curve; it is the standard CSS/animation control surface for timing [FACT-source: https://www.joshwcomeau.com/animation/a-friendly-introduction-to-spring-physics/]. graphux specifies the drop/rise/decay as named easing curves, values left to the tuning surface rather than asserted.

included: cubic-bezier as four-control-point timing curve
curves as named, tunable, not hardcoded constants
excluded: the render cost of the curve (kb3)

pros.claim: A bezier vocabulary gives a compact, portable way to name the fall/rise/decay curves
pros.example: specifying the fall as an ease-in cubic-bezier the tuner fills in on the target device

cons.claim: A bezier cannot reproduce a true spring's settling oscillation, so it under-serves bouncy feel
cons.example: approximating a bouncy water settle with a bezier and losing the multi-bounce read

failure_modes: asserting exact bezier constants as facts before tuning
forcing a bouncy motion onto a curve that cannot oscillate
acceptance_tests: the drop/rise/decay are named as tunable easing curves with constants deferred to measurement
revisit_triggers: a spring feel is required that a bezier cannot express

base.update_signal: a required spring feel exceeds what a bezier can express

nodes.definition: A spring is parameterised by mass, stiffness, and damping and produces a DECAYING OSCILLATION — it overshoots and settles over multiple bounces with no fixed end-time [FACT-source: https://www.joshwcomeau.com/animation/a-friendly-introduction-to-spring-physics/]. Springs give the most lifelike water settle and splash recoil; their open-ended duration is both their charm and a pacing risk.

included: spring as mass/stiffness/damping decaying oscillation
no fixed end-time as charm and pacing risk
excluded: the CSS approximation route (kb3 CSS linear())
the honesty of the settled level (kb2)

pros.claim: A spring gives the water settle and splash recoil a natural, alive quality a fixed curve cannot
pros.example: a lightly-damped spring on the water surface so it ripples and settles believably after a hit

cons.claim: A spring's open-ended settling can extend a beat unpredictably and cost frames if hand-rolled naively
cons.example: an under-damped spring that keeps oscillating and delays the next drop

failure_modes: an under-damped spring that never visually settles
hand-rolling a spring loop that blows the frame budget
acceptance_tests: springs are specified with mass/stiffness/damping and a settling threshold so the beat has a practical end
revisit_triggers: a spring's settling time conflicts with the reward-beat pacing

base.update_signal: spring settling time conflicts with reward-beat pacing

nodes.definition: A bezier can only APPROXIMATE a spring; the multi-point CSS linear() timing function closes part of the gap by sampling a spring curve into many points [FACT-source: https://www.carmenansio.com/articles/spring-physics-css/]. This node is the explicit decision surface: which drill motions need true spring behaviour vs a cheaper bezier/linear() approximation.

included: bezier-approximates-spring and the linear() bridge
per-motion choice of spring vs approximation

pros.claim: Naming the tradeoff per motion avoids paying spring cost where a bezier reads identically
pros.example: using a bezier for the drop fall and reserving spring/linear() for the water settle only

cons.claim: The choice cannot be settled on aesthetics alone; it interacts with the unmeasured performance envelope
cons.example: picking springs everywhere before measuring their cost on the target device

failure_modes: choosing springs everywhere without a cost measurement
using a flat bezier where a settle needs oscillation
acceptance_tests: each drill motion is assigned spring vs bezier/linear() with the choice tied to a measured cost, not asserted
revisit_triggers: a measurement shows the spring approximation is indistinguishable or too costly

base.update_signal: a benchmark revises which motions justify true spring behaviour

nodes.definition: The drop's fall is an ease-in (accelerating) curve evoking gravity, spanning the fall window. Critically, the curve's DURATION is not graphux's to shorten: it is floored by qcraft's ESL-readable window (kb2). graphux owns the SHAPE of the fall within that duration, never its floor.

included: ease-in gravity shape for the fall
shape owned by graphux, duration floored by the ESL window

pros.claim: Separating fall SHAPE from fall DURATION lets feel improve without ever threatening the readability floor
pros.example: making the fall accelerate for drama while keeping its total time at or above the ESL floor

cons.claim: A dramatic gravity curve can create the illusion of less reading time near the end of the fall
cons.example: a hard late acceleration that makes the last options feel rushed even though total time is safe

failure_modes: shortening the fall to feel snappier and breaching the ESL floor
letting the drop become the selection target
acceptance_tests: the fall is an ease-in shape whose duration is >= the ESL floor in every path, verified against qcraft's estimate
revisit_triggers: a pacing request would push the fall at or below the ESL floor

base.update_signal: a pacing change pushes the fall duration toward the ESL floor

nodes.definition: On a genuine correct-in-window hit the water rises by one quantized step (viz's floored increment) with an ease-out settle and a brief surface ripple. The rise animates BETWEEN discrete honest steps; it must never render a smooth continuous fill that implies a measured continuum (kb2 / viz dominance).

included: ease-out settle + ripple on a stepped rise
animating between discrete steps, never a smooth continuum
excluded: the number of steps and the hue token (viz)
the correctness rule that triggers a rise (engage)

pros.claim: Animating between quantized steps keeps the meter honest while still feeling fluid
pros.example: a quick ease-out rise from step 6 to step 7 with a settle ripple, no in-between continuous value shown

cons.claim: A fluid rise animation can visually imply sub-step precision the counter does not have
cons.example: an overshoot that momentarily shows the water above the true step and reads as extra progress

failure_modes: a smooth continuous fill that fakes a measured continuum
an overshoot that misreads the honest step value
acceptance_tests: the rise animates between viz's discrete steps with an ease-out settle and never displays a between-step continuum
revisit_triggers: the rise is found to imply sub-step precision

base.update_signal: a review finds the rise implies sub-step precision

nodes.definition: The meter decays over time when idle; the DECAY ANIMATION is framed as session momentum ('use it or lose it this session'), NOT forgetting/retrievability — borrowing the FSRS forgetting concept would be dishonest [FACT — GAMIFICATION_PLAN §1]. The decay curve is a gentle, continuous-looking drain rendered still against the stepped scale; its timescale is session-only, never multi-day.

included: decay as session-momentum drain, not forgetting
session-only timescale, honest framing
excluded: the decay rate constant (engage / open decision)

pros.claim: A session-only momentum framing keeps the decay from falsely implying memory loss or pulling early review
pros.example: a slow drain that resets at session end and is labelled momentum, not memory

cons.claim: Any decay animation risks reading as 'you are forgetting', the exact dishonest borrow to avoid
cons.example: a drain styled like a depleting knowledge bar that implies retrievability loss

failure_modes: framing decay as forgetting/retrievability
a multi-day decay that pulls the user to review early and breaks spacing
acceptance_tests: decay is animated as session-only momentum, never labelled or styled as forgetting, and never persists across days
revisit_triggers: a decay-timescale decision would make decay span days

base.update_signal: the water_decay_timescale decision changes decay across sessions

nodes.definition: A splash/particle burst on a hit is pure polish confirming a genuine correct-in-window event. Its scale should read from the drop's impact (SQUASH_AND_STRETCH) and its particle count is budgeted for both performance (kb3) and seizure safety — bursts must respect WCAG 2.3.1 three-flash limits (kb2).

included: splash burst as confirmation polish
particle count budgeted for perf and flash safety

pros.claim: A small splash gives a satisfying, legible confirmation of a real hit
pros.example: a short particle spray on the correct-in-window hit that decays within a few frames

cons.claim: Particle bursts are the highest flash-safety and performance risk element in the drill
cons.example: a bright, rapidly flashing burst that could approach the three-flash seizure threshold

failure_modes: a flashing burst that risks the seizure limit
an unbudgeted particle count that janks on the target device
acceptance_tests: the splash burst is capped for particle count and verified against the three-flash limit before ship
revisit_triggers: a burst is found near the flash threshold or over the frame budget

base.update_signal: a flash-safety or performance check flags the burst

nodes.definition: The feedback sequence is choreographed: tap -> immediate button ACK (<~100ms) -> water rise + splash reward beat (longer). The ACK confirms control; the beat confirms outcome. Sequencing keeps the drill responsive without rushing either the readable window or the reward.

included: tap->ack->reward-beat sequencing
fast ack, deliberate reward beat

pros.claim: Choreographing ack and reward separately gives responsiveness AND a satisfying beat
pros.example: the button confirms instantly while the water rise plays over the following moments

cons.claim: A long reward beat can delay the next drop and stall the drill's rhythm
cons.example: a splash+rise so long the learner waits idle before the next item

failure_modes: fusing ack and reward so the control feels laggy
a reward beat that stalls the drill cadence
acceptance_tests: the sequence separates a sub-~100ms ack from a longer reward beat and does not stall the next item
revisit_triggers: a playtest finds the reward beat stalls cadence

base.update_signal: a cadence playtest revises the beat timing

nodes.definition: Every motion in the drill must map to a REAL event: the rise only on genuine correctness-in-window, the splash only on that same hit, the decay only on real idle time. Motion that fires without a genuine event manufactures feedback and, if it reads as progress, breaches the honesty contract (kb2).

included: one-motion-per-real-event discipline
no manufactured feedback
excluded: the correctness rule that defines the event (engage)

pros.claim: Tying each motion to a real event keeps the feel honest and the feedback trustworthy
pros.example: suppressing the rise entirely on a timeout since no genuine in-window hit occurred

cons.claim: Strict event-mapping can feel less lively than free-floating ambient motion
cons.example: resisting an idle ambient shimmer because it maps to no event, at some cost to liveliness

failure_modes: ambient motion that reads as feedback without an event
rewarding motion/speed alone with a rise
acceptance_tests: each motion is bound to a genuine event and none fires on speed or motion alone
revisit_triggers: a proposed effect maps to no genuine drill event

base.update_signal: an effect is proposed that maps to no genuine event

nodes.definition: The tunable feel surface — fall ease shape, rise settle stiffness, decay curve, splash scale/count, ack latency — is a set of parameters whose VALUES are UNKNOWN until prototyped and tuned on the target device [UNKNOWN — no values asserted]. graphux presents the surface and the tuning method, never asserts constants.

included: the parameter surface as a tuning target
values deferred to measurement, never asserted
excluded: the honesty limits on each parameter (kb2)

pros.claim: Exposing feel as a named parameter surface makes tuning systematic and honest about what is unknown
pros.example: handing the tuner a list of curves to fill in rather than shipping guessed constants

cons.claim: An open parameter surface can be tuned toward juice that breaches the honesty or ESL limits
cons.example: tuning the fall shorter for snappiness until it nears the ESL floor

failure_modes: asserting tuned constants as facts before measurement
tuning past the honesty/ESL limits for feel
acceptance_tests: the feel parameters are listed with values marked UNKNOWN-until-tuned and bounded by the honesty/ESL/perf limits
revisit_triggers: tuning results arrive and replace the UNKNOWN values

base.update_signal: device tuning replaces the UNKNOWN parameter values

nodes.definition: Synthesis: emit a feel specification for the drill whose every motion (fall, rise, decay, splash, squash) is grounded in a named principle/curve, mapped to a real event, bounded by the honesty and ESL contracts, and whose external claims and tuning constants carry FACT-source / UNVERIFIED-SOURCE / UNKNOWN labels. This node closes kb1 and hands to kb2 (permission) and kb3 (feasibility).

included: the assembled, labelled feel spec
handoff to the permission and feasibility layers

pros.claim: A single labelled feel spec makes the drill's motion defensible, honest, and ready for the constraint/perf gates
pros.example: emitting the fall/rise/decay/splash spec with each external number tagged and each motion event-bound

cons.claim: The synthesis is only as honest as its labels; an unlabelled asserted constant poisons it
cons.example: letting one tuned duration slip in as a FACT without the UNKNOWN-until-tuned tag

failure_modes: shipping a feel spec with unlabelled external or tuned numbers
omitting the honesty/ESL bounds from the spec
acceptance_tests: the feel spec labels every external claim and tuned constant and carries the honesty/ESL/perf bounds forward
revisit_triggers: a downstream gate rejects an unlabelled claim in the spec

base.update_signal: a downstream gate revises the feel synthesis

edges.why_related: real-time control is the first decomposed element of game feel
simulated space is the second decomposed element of game feel
polish/juice is the third decomposed element of game feel
the classic principles are the grammar the feel frame draws on
the restraint rule bounds the polish layer
squash-stretch is a principle in the catalogue
easing is a principle in the catalogue
the easing principle is implemented via curve vocabulary
springs extend the curve vocabulary to oscillation
the tradeoff is framed over the curve vocabulary
the tradeoff weighs springs against beziers
the fall curve applies the easing principle
the fall is expressed as an easing curve
the rise settle uses spring/ease-out behaviour
the rise moves the simulated water object
decay follows the rise on the same meter
the splash scale reads from squash-stretch impact
the splash is a polish-layer element
the ack target sets the head of the choreography
the rise is the reward beat in the choreography

the verdict includes the fall spec
the verdict includes the decay spec

conflict_axes.name: cinematic_pacing_vs_esl_readable_floor
conflict_axes.description: A dramatic, slow-building fall feels better but the fall duration is floored by the ESL-readable window; lengthening is allowed, undercutting is not.
poles: lengthen the fall for cinematic drama
never let feel shorten the fall below the ESL floor
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: feel may lengthen the fall but the ESL floor dominates: the readable window is never traded for pacing

conflict_axes.name: juice_richness_vs_information_legibility
conflict_axes.description: Richer juice (shake, particles, overshoot) is more satisfying but can obscure which option was chosen or the true step value.
poles: keep the correctness and level reads unobstructed
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: legibility dominates: cut any effect that obscures the choice or the honest step, per the restraint rule

conflict_axes.name: smooth_fluid_rise_vs_quantized_honesty
conflict_axes.description: A smooth continuous fill feels fluid but implies a measured continuum the counter lacks.
poles: animate only between discrete honest steps
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: quantized honesty dominates: the rise animates between viz's floored steps and never shows a between-step continuum

conflict_axes.name: spring_liveliness_vs_frame_budget
conflict_axes.description: Springs give the most lifelike settle but their open-ended oscillation can cost frames if hand-rolled.
poles: cap spring use to what the frame budget allows
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the measured frame budget dominates: reserve springs for motions that justify their measured cost

conflict_axes.name: celebratory_burst_vs_no_mastery_implication
conflict_axes.description: A big celebratory burst is rewarding but can read as durable mastery/level-up rather than a session hit.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the no-mastery-implication contract dominates: no burst may read as durable progress

conflict_axes.name: decay_drama_vs_honest_momentum_framing
conflict_axes.description: A dramatic depleting-bar decay is compelling but reads as forgetting/retrievability loss.
poles: dramatic depletion styled like memory loss
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: honest framing dominates: decay is session momentum, never forgetting, never multi-day

conflict_axes.name: fast_snappy_beat_vs_readable_reward
conflict_axes.description: A fast beat feels snappy but can rush the reward read or the fall window.
poles: compress the whole beat for snappiness
fast ack, but a readable reward and window
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the ack is fast while the reward beat and fall window stay readable; snappiness never compresses reading time

conflict_axes.name: asserted_feel_constants_vs_measured_tuning
conflict_axes.description: Shipping guessed feel constants is faster than prototyping, but the app has no motion history to assert from.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: measured tuning dominates: feel constants are UNKNOWN until tuned on the target device

conflict_axes.name: liveliness_vs_strict_event_mapping
conflict_axes.description: Ambient free-floating motion adds life but can read as feedback without a real event.
poles: every motion maps to a genuine event
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: event-mapping dominates: liveliness may not manufacture feedback that reads as progress

edge_cases.description: The learner has prefers-reduced-motion set, so the fall/rise/splash are all removed.
edge_cases.mitigation: fall back to a static countdown numeral/ring + stepped meter that conveys 100% of the timer information (handled by kb2)

edge_cases.description: A hit lands in the final frames of the fall, so the rise must trigger while the fall is still animating.
edge_cases.trigger: a correct-in-window tap near fall end
edge_cases.mitigation: cleanly interrupt the fall, ack the tap immediately, and start the rise without a visual glitch

edge_cases.description: A spring water-settle keeps oscillating and overlaps the next drop's spawn.
edge_cases.mitigation: raise damping or apply a settle threshold so the beat ends before the next item

edge_cases.description: The splash particle burst flashes brightly several times in quick succession.
edge_cases.mitigation: cap flashes below the three-flash seizure limit and reduce burst brightness/frequency

edge_cases.description: A dramatic late gravity acceleration makes the last option feel unreadable though total time is safe.
edge_cases.mitigation: soften the late acceleration so perceived reading time matches the safe total duration

edge_cases.description: A designer proposes an idle ambient shimmer with no triggering event.
edge_cases.mitigation: reject or bind the shimmer to a genuine event so it cannot read as feedback

edge_cases.description: The rise overshoots and momentarily shows water above the true quantized step.
edge_cases.mitigation: clamp the overshoot or damp it so the displayed level never exceeds the honest step

edge_cases.description: A tuner ships a guessed fall duration as a hard constant before any device measurement.
edge_cases.mitigation: revert to UNKNOWN-until-tuned and require a target-device measurement before the constant ships

edge_cases.description: The decay animation is styled as a depleting knowledge bar.
edge_cases.mitigation: restyle as session momentum and relabel; never imply retrievability loss

edge_cases.description: The reward beat is so long the next drop is delayed and the drill cadence stalls.
edge_cases.mitigation: shorten the reward beat while keeping the ack fast and the window readable

edge_cases.description: A bezier is used for a motion that visibly needs spring oscillation and reads as flat.
edge_cases.trigger: bezier where a spring is needed
edge_cases.mitigation: switch that motion to a spring or CSS linear() approximation after a cost check

workflow.action: Frame the feel request and scope it to the drill
workflow.description: State the motion as real-time control + simulated space + polish over the drop/water/tank, and confirm the mechanic/encoding/copy are inputs not outputs.
workflow.gate: the request is scoped to drill feel and the sibling inputs are named before any curve is chosen

workflow.action: Ground each motion in a principle and curve
workflow.description: Map the fall/rise/splash to squash-stretch, anticipation, easing, and name the bezier/spring curve for each.
workflow.gate: every motion is tied to a named principle and a named tunable curve

workflow.action: Set the fall shape within the ESL-floored duration
workflow.description: Specify the ease-in fall shape and confirm its duration is >= the ESL floor in every path.
workflow.gate: the fall duration is verified >= the ESL floor before the shape is finalised

workflow.action: Specify the stepped rise and honest settle
workflow.description: Animate the rise between viz's discrete steps with an ease-out settle and no between-step continuum or overshoot beyond the step.
workflow.gate: the rise never displays a smooth continuum or an over-step overshoot

workflow.description: Specify a session-only momentum drain, never forgetting, never multi-day.
workflow.gate: decay is session-scoped and honestly framed

workflow.action: Budget the splash for legibility, flash, and perf
workflow.description: Cap particle count and brightness for the frame budget and the three-flash seizure limit.
workflow.gate: the splash clears flash safety and the frame budget

workflow.description: Sequence a sub-~100ms button ack ahead of the longer reward beat without stalling cadence.
workflow.gate: ack is fast, the reward beat and window stay readable, cadence holds

workflow.description: Bind every motion to a genuine event; reject any effect that fires on speed/motion alone or reads as mastery.
workflow.gate: no motion fires without a real event or implies durable progress

workflow.action: Expose the tuning surface with values UNKNOWN
workflow.description: List the feel parameters, mark values UNKNOWN-until-tuned, and bound them by the honesty/ESL/perf limits.
workflow.gate: every feel constant is deferred to measurement and bounded

workflow.description: Assemble the feel spec with FACT-source/UNVERIFIED-SOURCE/UNKNOWN labels on every external and tuned value and the honesty/ESL/perf bounds carried forward.
workflow.gate: every external and tuned value is labelled and the constraint bounds travel with the spec

dominance_rules.rule: The ESL-readable fall floor dominates cinematic pacing
dominance_rules.rationale: a fall shortened below the floor silently tests English reading rate, defeating the item
dominance_rules.trigger: a pacing change would push the fall at/below the ESL floor
dominance_rules.action: keep the floor; lengthen for drama only, never undercut

dominance_rules.rule: Quantized honesty dominates a smooth fluid rise
dominance_rules.rationale: a continuous fill implies a measured continuum the counter lacks
dominance_rules.trigger: a rise animation shows a between-step value
dominance_rules.action: animate only between viz's discrete steps

dominance_rules.rule: The honesty contract dominates celebratory juice
dominance_rules.rationale: a burst reading as mastery falsely signals durable progress
dominance_rules.action: scope feedback to the session and strip mastery connotation

dominance_rules.rationale: motion without an event manufactures feedback
dominance_rules.trigger: an effect maps to no genuine event
dominance_rules.action: bind it to an event or cut it

dominance_rules.rule: The measured frame budget dominates spring liveliness
dominance_rules.rationale: an open-ended spring can blow the budget if hand-rolled
dominance_rules.trigger: a spring's cost is unmeasured or over budget
dominance_rules.action: cap spring use to measured-affordable motions

dominance_rules.rule: Honest session-momentum framing dominates decay drama
dominance_rules.rationale: a memory-loss styling borrows the FSRS forgetting concept dishonestly
dominance_rules.trigger: decay is styled or labelled as forgetting

dominance_rules.rule: Measured tuning dominates asserted feel constants
dominance_rules.rationale: the app has no motion history to assert constants from
dominance_rules.trigger: a feel constant is asserted before measurement
dominance_rules.action: mark UNKNOWN-until-tuned and measure on the target device

dominance_rules.rationale: juice that hides the choice or step defeats its own purpose
dominance_rules.trigger: an effect obscures the correctness or level read
dominance_rules.action: cut or reduce the effect until the read is clear

dominance_rules.rule: A fast ack dominates a compressed beat
dominance_rules.rationale: control feel needs the ack fast even when the reward is deliberately slow
dominance_rules.trigger: the beat is compressed and the control feels laggy
dominance_rules.action: keep the ack sub-~100ms and pace the reward separately

anti_rework_rules.rule: Verify the fall duration against the ESL floor before finalising the fall shape
anti_rework_rules.prevents: rebuilding the fall after it is found to breach the readable window

anti_rework_rules.rule: Animate the rise between quantized steps from the start
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-authoring a smooth fill that was found to imply false precision

anti_rework_rules.rule: Frame decay as session momentum before styling it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-styling a decay that shipped as a memory-loss bar

anti_rework_rules.rule: Budget splash particle count and flashes before implementation
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-doing a burst that failed flash-safety or the frame budget

anti_rework_rules.rule: Mark every feel constant UNKNOWN-until-tuned before handoff
anti_rework_rules.prevents: reverting asserted constants after a device measurement contradicts them

anti_rework_rules.rule: Bind every motion to a real event during design
anti_rework_rules.prevents: stripping ambient effects later that were found to manufacture feedback

anti_rework_rules.rule: Separate ack latency from reward-beat pacing up front
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-choreographing after the control is found to feel laggy

anti_rework_rules.rule: Tag every external motion claim FACT-source/UNVERIFIED-SOURCE at authoring time
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-auditing the spec later for unlabelled snippet-grade claims

iteration_protocol.trigger: a live source check confirms or revises the ~100ms response target and the 12-principle/spring/bezier attributions (all snippet-grade here)
iteration_protocol.action: replace UNVERIFIED-SOURCE tags with cited FACTs and re-check any curve that leaned on a revised figure

iteration_protocol.trigger: target-device tuning produces measured feel constants
iteration_protocol.action: replace UNKNOWN feel-parameter values with measured constants and re-verify the ESL floor and frame budget

iteration_protocol.trigger: a motion/animation library is prototyped and benchmarked
iteration_protocol.action: revise the spring-vs-bezier tradeoff and the simulation model against the measured verdict

iteration_protocol.trigger: qcraft revises the ESL-readable floor estimate
iteration_protocol.action: re-check the fall-shape spec against the new floor

iteration_protocol.trigger: viz revises the step count or hue token
iteration_protocol.action: re-check the rise/decay animation against the new quantization

iteration_protocol.trigger: a playtest reveals cadence or legibility problems
iteration_protocol.action: re-choreograph the beat and re-budget the juice

priority_rationale: The game-feel frame and the classic principles come first because they fix the vocabulary and grammar every curve refines; the fall/rise/decay/splash specs and the honesty-bounded tuning surface follow, and the labelled verdict closes the layer for the permission (kb2) and feasibility (kb3) gates.
